pats_add.title: The Bank's business ranking, with four countries' data changed
pats_add.summary:
Doing Business was the World Bank's annual ranking of 190 countries on how easy they made it to start and run a company. Investors used it, and governments rewrote laws to climb it. The Bank suspended it in August 2020 and commissioned the law firm WilmerHale to investigate how its numbers had been produced; the report went to the Bank's board of executive directors on 15 September 2021, and the Bank cancelled the ranking.

The report found that data had been changed improperly for four countries across two editions: China in Doing Business 2018, and Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Azerbaijan in Doing Business 2020. China's score was raised while the Bank was negotiating a capital increase in which China's support mattered; the changes put China at 78th, seven places above what the draft data gave. The investigators found that staff made the China changes under pressure from the office of the Bank's president, Jim Yong Kim, and from Kristalina Georgieva, then the Bank's chief executive; Georgieva said she disagreed fundamentally with the findings, and in October 2021 the board of the IMF, which she now heads, backed her.

For the 2020 edition the first step was not about money. In September 2019 Simeon Djankov, then the Bank's director for development economics, told the Doing Business team to find a way to drop Jordan from the top of the draft Top Improvers list, explaining, according to one manager on the team, that the economic and social pressures Jordan was under would make the report not credible with Jordan as top reformer. An employee sent to Jordan reported that Jordan's data was correct, and the team then looked for ways to lift Saudi Arabia past it. Saudi Arabia rose 30 places to 62nd and was named top improver, and it had been paying the Bank for advisory work on the very indicators being scored. The report's finding is that the Saudi and Emirati changes were likely an effort by a senior Bank staff member to reward Saudi Arabia for its role in the Bank community, including those paid contracts, and it lists the contracts as one of three things that could have motivated him, alongside a speech he gave in Riyadh in January 2019 and talks at a reformers' club. The Emirati data was changed because that country's tax system resembled Saudi Arabia's, and the change did not move its ranking. Azerbaijan's data was changed the other way and no money appears in it: three reforms its own internal audit had confirmed were left uncounted at Djankov's direction, cutting the score by nearly two points and dropping the country off the Top Improvers list, on his stated disbelief that the reforms were real, with multiple employees telling the investigators he appeared to harbour a personal animus against the country. For neither the Saudi nor the Azerbaijan changes did the investigators find evidence that the president's office or the board was involved.

The scoring also shaped law. Until 2009 the ranking scored countries higher for weaker protections for workers, through what was called the employing workers indicator. The Bank suspended that indicator in 2009 after pressure from trade unions, the International Labour Organization and the US Congress, and a panel the Bank set up in 2013 recommended removing it permanently. Warnings had come from inside as well: in January 2018 the Bank's chief economist, Paul Romer, said Chile had fallen in the rankings because of changes in method rather than changes in Chile, and suggested politics might be behind it; he then said he had not meant to suggest manipulation and resigned, and Augusto Lopez-Claros, who had directed the group that published the ranking, called the claim that the changes targeted Chile wholly without merit.
pats_add.implications:
Both changes that moved a country up favoured a country whose money or support the Bank needed at the time: China during a capital increase, Saudi Arabia while paying the Bank for advice on the indicators being scored. The report does not find that the money caused either change; for Saudi Arabia it puts the reward motive as likely and names the paid contracts as one factor among three, and for Azerbaijan it finds no money at all. It also records that employees raised a concern that the Bank's paid advisory work "can lead to the impression of a pay-to-play scheme" - an impression employees reported, not a finding of the investigation.

For a reader the practical point is who the numbers served. A ranking that governments changed labour and tax law to climb was, in these two editions, partly set by what senior managers at the lender wanted, in one case to please a government and in another on one official's private view of a country. The people affected were never party to any of it: the employing workers indicator rewarded cutting protections for workers in every country scored, for six years before it was suspended. The Bank's replacement ranking, Business Ready, launched in 2024 and brings a labour topic back, so the same question applies to it.

pats_add.title: Loans arranged by banks and traders and kept off the public books
pats_add.summary:
Governments are supposed to record what they owe, and lenders such as the IMF set limits on new borrowing as a condition of their own loans. In several countries loans arranged by international banks and commodity traders were kept out of those records, and surfaced only when the country could not pay.

Mozambique is the case a regulator has written up. Between 2013 and 2014 three companies tied to the Mozambican state borrowed about $2 billion through Credit Suisse and Russia's VTB, nominally for a tuna fleet and coastal security, without the approval of Mozambique's parliament. The Financial Conduct Authority's final notice of 19 October 2021, which fined Credit Suisse 147,190,200 pounds, records that the bank understood the government would only represent in general terms that it had complied with its IMF obligations, "rather than undertake to inform the IMF of the loans in question", and that in January 2014 the purported purpose of the first loan was still not public knowledge. The US Department of Justice, in a $547 million coordinated settlement the same month, said about $200 million of the borrowed money went in bribes and kickbacks, about $50 million of it to Credit Suisse bankers; Credit Suisse admitted fraud and cancelled $200 million of Mozambique's debt. A study by Mozambique's Centre for Public Integrity and Norway's Chr. Michelsen Institute put the cost to the economy at $11 billion and found the slowdown pushed nearly two million people into poverty.

The World Bank's own board paper on debt vulnerabilities in IDA countries, dated 4 October 2018, treats this as recurring rather than singular. Its box on hidden debt opens by saying there have been several recent cases of hidden debt among IDA countries and names three: in the Republic of Congo, pre-financing contracts with oil traders contracted by the state oil company on the government's behalf but left undisclosed to the debt management office for over two years; in Togo, pre-financed debt in 2015 amounting to 7 per cent of GDP at the end of 2016 and absent from official debt statistics; and in Mozambique, the two state guarantees of 2013 and 2014 worth $1.15 billion, 9 per cent of GDP at the end of 2015, not disclosed to debt management staff or the public. Of those three the Bank names a type of arranger only for Congo, so the banks-and-traders part of this pattern rests on the named firms in particular countries rather than on the Bank's box.

Those firms are named elsewhere. In Congo, Glencore and Trafigura had lent against future oil; the IMF raised its estimate of Congo's debt from 77 to 110 per cent of national income during 2017 as hidden debts came to light, and Global Witness later found up to $3.3 billion more carried by the state oil company that had never been disclosed. In Chad, the joint World Bank and IMF debt sustainability analysis of July 2019 records that a Glencore loan accounted for about 98 per cent of the country's commercial debt stock in 2017, and that in 2016 $231 million of the government's $271 million in net oil revenue, about 85 per cent, went to Glencore. In Europe, Goldman Sachs arranged currency swaps for Greece in 2001 that hid about 2.8 billion euros of debt after Greece had joined the single currency; Goldman said the swaps were legal under the rules of the time. For Chinese lending the gap has been measured: AidData reported in 2021 about $385 billion of debt tied to Chinese lenders that borrowing governments had not reported, mostly because it was owed by state companies and special-purpose firms rather than by the government itself.
pats_add.implications:
Hidden lending works because the official record is built from what governments choose to report: the World Bank's debt register relies on borrower returns, loans to state companies are often left out, and trader pre-payment deals are private contracts. The arranger is paid its fees at the start, out of the loan. The cost falls later and on people who were never told: Mozambique was cut off from donor funding and defaulted, Chad handed most of one year's net oil revenue to a single trader, and Congo's debt figure jumped by a third of national income in a year.

No comparable count exists for Western banks and commodity traders. AidData measured the Chinese gap by comparing what lenders recorded against what borrowers reported; nobody has done that for bank and trader lending, so how much of the world's sovereign debt is missing from the official numbers is unknown. What is established is narrower and still substantial: the lender's own board paper says several of its poorest borrowers carried debts their own debt offices did not know about, and in the one case a regulator has examined in full, the bank knew the loans were being kept from the IMF and arranged them anyway.

pats_add.title: Companies paying soldiers and armed groups where they operate
pats_add.summary:
Two foreign companies have pleaded guilty in US courts to paying armed groups designated as terrorists, a third's payments to an army came out through its own records, and a fourth has disclosed payments for state security in every annual report for nine years running.

Chiquita Brands, the American banana company, pleaded guilty on 19 March 2007 to making payments to the United Self-Defence Forces of Colombia, the AUC. The Justice Department's release records over 100 payments totalling over $1.7 million through its Colombian subsidiary Banadex between 1997 and 4 February 2004, in the banana regions of Uraba and Santa Marta where the AUC was killing civilians; 50 payments of over $825,000 after the AUC was designated a terrorist organisation in September 2001; and 20 payments of over $300,000 after Chiquita's own board member and outside counsel had disclosed the payments to the Justice Department and been told they were illegal. The payments were booked as security payments, and the release states that Chiquita never received any actual security services for them. Chiquita paid a $25 million fine. The same release records that the payments were demanded: they began after a 1997 meeting between the AUC's then leader, Carlos Castano, and a senior Banadex executive, at which Castano implied that failure to pay could result in physical harm to Banadex personnel and property, and when Chiquita came forward it "represented that the payments had been made under threat of violence". Its own outside counsel advised that it could not do indirectly what it could not do directly, that a defence of duress would weaken if the payments continued, and that the company should leave Colombia; it stayed and kept paying. In June 2024 a federal jury in Florida found Chiquita liable for eight killings by the AUC and ordered it to pay $38.3 million to the families.

In October 2022 the French cement company Lafarge pleaded guilty in the United States to paying the Islamic State and the al-Nusrah Front, through intermediaries, about $6 million in 2013 and 2014 to keep its $680 million plant in northern Syria running, and agreed to pay about $778 million. US officials said it was the first time a company had pleaded guilty to conspiring to provide material support to a foreign terrorist organisation.

Payments to state forces are the larger part and are mostly legal. In December 2005 the New York Times reported, from company records, that Freeport-McMoRan had given Indonesian military and police generals, colonels, majors, captains and units nearly $20 million between 1998 and 2004 around its Grasberg copper and gold mine in Papua, besides money for barracks and roads; Freeport said it had no alternative to relying on Indonesia's military and police and that the payments were legal. It still discloses them: a search of the US Securities and Exchange Commission's full-text index returns the phrase "support costs for government-provided security" in nine consecutive Freeport annual reports on Form 10-K, for the financial years 2017 to 2025, filed between February 2018 and February 2026. In 2017 Amnesty International published a report drawn from thousands of pages of Shell's internal documents from Nigeria in the 1990s, when the Ogoni were protesting against the company's oil pollution. Amnesty found that Shell gave the security forces logistical support and payments, which the head of Shell Nigeria from 1994 accepted was standard practice, and that it kept requesting military help after security forces had killed protesters and burned villages; Shell says it never colluded with the military or encouraged violence.
pats_add.implications:
Who benefits is visible in the accounting. For Chiquita the payments were a cost of staying in the banana regions, booked as security and bought nothing the company could point to; the AUC was killing people in the same places, and eighteen years later a jury made the company pay for eight of those deaths. For Freeport the payments keep a mine open in a territory under military occupation, and they are not a scandal the company has had to deny: they appear in its annual report every year, defended as having no alternative. That is the difference between the two kinds of case. Prosecutions reach the payments to groups a government has designated; payments to that government's own soldiers and police are ordinary disclosed business, even where those forces have killed people near the site - in April 1995 the Australian Council for Overseas Aid reported at least 37 people killed or disappeared around the Grasberg mine, 22 of them civilians, with Freeport and the Indonesian government denying the figures.

In Colombia and Syria the armed groups demanded the money under threat, which is the companies' defence and is in the prosecutors' own record. It did not excuse them: the outside counsel's advice recorded in the Justice Department's release warns that a duress defence weakens the longer the payments continue, and both companies kept paying after being told to stop. Nothing requires a company to publish what it pays to soldiers, police or armed groups abroad, so how common the practice is cannot be counted; what can be seen is that where it has come out, it came out through a prosecution, a newspaper's access to company records, or a rights group's access to internal files.

pats_add.uncertain: No disclosure requirement exists for company payments to soldiers, police or armed groups abroad, so the practice cannot be counted and nothing here says how common it is. The Freeport evidence is the SEC's own full-text index, not the filings themselves: sec.gov/Archives refuses requests from automated clients without a contact address, which was not invented, so the nine filings were confirmed by their index entries and the matched phrase, and no amount disclosed in those filings is given here. EDGAR's full-text index does not reach filings before 2001, so the phrase may appear in earlier years than 2017 without showing in this search. The nearly $20 million for 1998-2004 is the New York Times's reading of company records. Amnesty's Nigerian findings rest on documents it obtained, and Shell denies collusion. Whether Chiquita's payments are best read as extortion or as buying protection is contested: the prosecutors recorded both the threat and the company's decision to keep paying after being told to stop.

pats_add.title: City water put into private hands in projects the World Bank designed to bring companies in
pats_add.summary:
The World Bank's own evaluators counted this across the Bank's portfolio. In Water and Development, published by the Independent Evaluation Group on 30 June 2010, the evaluation states that thirteen per cent of the Bank's projects dealing with urban water supply and sanitation aimed to introduce private sector participation, that seventy of those projects had closed, and that forty-six had managed to involve the private sector as planned by the time they closed. Of the twenty-four that did not, Turkey and Venezuela ended their contracts early, six countries - Algeria, Argentina, Nigeria, Rwanda, Tunisia and Uganda - cancelled one or two contracts out of several, and Bolivia cancelled all of its contracts. The same chapter records who took which work: international private firms tend to focus on large and medium-size cities, while small-scale local operators have the advantage in remoter areas, which international firms tend to ignore.

So the design is the Bank's own, stated in its evaluators' words and counted in its own projects. What that produced in particular cities is documented case by case. In Manila, the Bank's private-sector arm, the International Finance Corporation, drafted the 1997 concession agreement under a contract that paid it at least $1 million if the bidding succeeded, and in 2004 bought into one of the winning companies. Basic rates in the east zone rose 496 per cent between 1997 and 2003; from late October 2003, 672 people in the poor Tondo district fell ill with gastroenteritis after the west zone operator, part-owned by France's Suez, allegedly lowered water pressure. Coverage did rise, from about 60 to over 80 per cent of people in Metro Manila by 2002.

In Jakarta the Bank's part was narrower than its own lending suggests. It lent the city's water company $92 million in 1991 and assigned consultants who advised privatisation, but the Bank's completion report on that loan, dated 23 June 1998, says in a single sentence that the privatisation of the city water company's operations was an event "parallel to but facilitated by the Project" and that it was not envisaged by the government or the Bank when the loan was appraised, because private participation was then a new concept; at paragraph 28 it adds that in the late 1980s, had the government proposed such an option, the Bank would most likely have turned it down after other unsuccessful experiences in Indonesia. In 1997, without open bidding, the city was split between Britain's Thames Water, whose local company gave 20 per cent to President Suharto's son, and Suez, partnered with the Salim Group of a Suharto associate. Tariffs rose by 35, 40 and 30 per cent in three years, and coverage reached only 59 per cent by 2015 against a 98 per cent target. In October 2017 Indonesia's Supreme Court found the privatisation had not improved water quality, quantity or continuity, and ordered it ended.

In Cochabamba, Bolivia gave the water system of its third city to Aguas del Tunari, controlled through offshore holdings by the American engineering company Bechtel, on a 40-year contract in September 1999, in a process with a single bidder. Bills rose by more than half on average and in some homes by up to 200 per cent, in a country whose minimum wage was about $60 a month. In April 2000 the government declared a state of siege, soldiers shot dead a 17-year-old, Victor Hugo Daza, more than a hundred people were wounded, and the company left. Its owners had moved its registration to the Netherlands, used a Dutch investment treaty to claim at least $50 million from Bolivia at the Bank's own arbitration centre, and dropped the claim in January 2006 for two bolivianos, about 30 cents.
pats_add.implications:
The gain and the loss sit in different places. The companies that took city water were a small group - Suez, Thames Water, Bechtel, Biwater - and they took the large and medium-size cities, where there are enough paying customers; the evaluation says the remoter places were left to small local operators or ignored. The households are where the price rose: 496 per cent in east Manila over six years, more than half on average in Cochabamba, three successive rises in Jakarta. The lender's arm that wrote the Manila contract was paid for the deal closing, not for what followed.

The Bank's evaluators also record that the programme did not do what it was for. They write that the formal private sector "has not played the investment role that had been hoped for" and that public providers remain the norm. Of the seventy closed projects aimed at bringing private operators in, twenty-four did not manage it, and three of the cities in this pattern ended in reversal: Bolivia cancelled every contract it had, Indonesia's Supreme Court ordered Jakarta's privatisation ended, and Manila's west zone operator tried to walk away from its concession. What the published record does not show is who drafted the advice in each city or which companies were consulted before the terms were set.

pats_add.title: Money for health put into for-profit care without checking who it reached
pats_add.summary:
Britain's independent aid scrutiny body, which reports to Parliament, has examined this inside one development finance institution. The Independent Commission for Aid Impact reviewed CDC Group, the UK government's investment arm, in March 2019. Health was 7 per cent of CDC's portfolio at the end of 2017, 258.8 million pounds, up from 6 per cent in 2011; between 2012 and the third quarter of 2017, 61 per cent of new CDC investments were made as direct equity, 22 per cent as direct debt and 17 per cent through funds. The finding that matters is about what was asked before the money went out. The commission reports that the investment committee papers for more than three-quarters of the investments in its sample did not consider which socio-economic groups would benefit. Its example is a health investment: the papers for an Indian fund targeting healthcare businesses argued the fund would improve the affordability of healthcare but did not consider which groups would benefit, and CDC later told the commission that the fund's initial commitment to target half low-income households had been "an ambition rather than a requirement", and that the funded services had largely reached those on above-average incomes.

Oxfam traced the same kind of money across five institutions. In 2023 it followed more than 350 health investments by the development finance arms of Britain, France, Germany, the European Union and the World Bank. It reported that the Nairobi Women's Hospital in Kenya, funded by several of them, had held patients - including a newborn baby and a schoolboy - for months until bills were paid, and had kept one woman's mother's body for two years; that at the funded Lagoon Hospitals in Lagos the most basic maternity package cost more than nine years' income for the poorest tenth of Nigerians; and that at CARE Hospitals in India, backed by three of the lenders, a family said their injured child was refused treatment unless they paid $1,200. TPG, a shareholder in that chain, told Oxfam patients are always treated in an emergency whatever their finances, and the International Finance Corporation told the Guardian that private providers can add to the capacity of health systems. Oxfam said it could not find a single disclosed evaluation that credibly measured what these investments did for low-income patients.

Where oversight has failed outright, it failed late. In early 2018 four investors in a $1 billion health fund - the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, the International Finance Corporation, CDC Group and France's Proparco - hired forensic accountants to find out what had happened to about $200 million they had put in to build hospitals and clinics in countries including Pakistan, India and Nigeria. The fund was run by the Abraaj Group, a Dubai private equity firm managing almost $14 billion. Abraaj collapsed within months in what Bloomberg called the largest private equity insolvency; in 2019 US prosecutors charged its founder, Arif Naqvi, and other executives with defrauding investors, and two former partners pleaded guilty. A British judge approved Naqvi's extradition in 2021 and the High Court refused his last challenge in March 2023. He denies the charges. The books were examined only after the investors noticed money sitting unspent.
pats_add.implications:
The institutions putting public money into for-profit health care could not say, from their own papers, who it would reach. That is the watchdog's finding, not a critic's: in more than three-quarters of the sample the question was not asked, and in the one health case it sets out, the answer when it was finally asked was that the services had gone mainly to patients on above-average incomes while the commitment to poor households had been treated as an aspiration. Oxfam, looking at more than 350 investments across five lenders, found no disclosed evaluation that measured the effect on low-income patients at all.

Who benefits turns on that gap. Fund managers are paid their fees whether or not the hospital serves poor patients, because nothing in the papers measures it; the hospitals earn from patients who can pay, and the cases Oxfam documents are of people who could not - detained until a bill was settled, or priced out of a birth. The lenders answer that private providers add capacity to weak health systems, which is a claim about hospitals existing, not about who gets into them. The Abraaj collapse shows what the same absence of checking looks like at the fund level: four public and philanthropic investors put about $200 million into a fund and found out what had happened to it by hiring accountants after the money stopped moving.

The poorest countries have been sued too, and two parliaments have legislated about it. A United Nations independent expert reported in 2010 that, on World Bank and IMF figures, 54 court cases had been brought by commercial creditors against 12 heavily indebted poor countries between 1998 and 2008. In 1999 Donegal International, registered in the British Virgin Islands, bought for about $3.2 million a debt with a principal of $29.8 million that Zambia owed Romania for farm machinery; when Zambia fell behind on a settlement Donegal sued in London in 2005 for more than $55 million, and in 2007 Zambia agreed to pay about $15.5 million, at a time when it was receiving debt relief from rich governments and the World Bank. The judge found Donegal's witnesses at times evasive and dishonest but held Zambia to the settlement. On 2 October 2012 a court in Ghana ordered the Argentine navy's training ship ARA Libertad held at the port of Tema, with more than 300 people aboard, over NML Capital's unpaid bonds; it sailed in December after the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea ordered Ghana to release it. Britain passed an Act in 2010 limiting what creditors can recover in its courts from the poorest countries, and Belgium passed a similar law in 2015, which NML Capital challenged and the Belgian Constitutional Court upheld.

The poorest-country cases show the same business running alongside debt relief. Donegal paid about $3.2 million for Zambia's old Romanian debt and was paid about $15.5 million while Zambia's other creditors were writing debt off, so relief given by governments and the World Bank freed money that a fund in a London court was able to claim. The UK's 2010 Act and Belgium's 2015 law exist because the courts of rich countries were where those claims succeeded; neither covers New York, where most sovereign bonds are governed and where, as above, no such law has yet passed.

The UK's 2010 Act and Belgium's 2015 law are recorded here, but what either has recovered or prevented in practice is not known, and no reply from Donegal beyond the 2007 judgment was found. The UN expert's 54 cases are that expert's report of World Bank and IMF figures for 1998 to 2008 and have not been updated. What the funds paid for the debt is almost never disclosed, so in the Zambian case the purchase price is the court's figure and in the Argentine cases it is not known.

The G20's suspension scheme of 2020 shows the same split between public and private lenders across all the countries that applied, on Debt Justice's reading of it. The Debt Service Suspension Initiative ran from May 2020 and asked private lenders to join voluntarily. Debt Justice, combining the IMF's September 2021 report with the World Bank's DSSI database, found that the 46 countries which applied had 23% of their external debt payments suspended between May 2020 and the end of June 2021: $10.3 billion suspended and $0.6 billion cancelled, against $36.4 billion that went on being paid. Other governments suspended 48% of the payments owed to them, multilateral institutions cancelled 5%, and private lenders suspended 0.2%, which was one Italian bank suspending payments by Zambia. Private creditors received $14.9 billion from those countries, more than any other creditor group; UK-based commercial lenders suspended nothing and received $3.2 billion, while China suspended $5.7 billion, over half the global total suspended. Zambia itself missed a $42.5 million interest payment and on 13 November 2020 became the first African country to default during the pandemic, and its 2021 budget gave more to debt payments than to education, health, water and sanitation together. Its bondholders settled only in 2024, in a deal Debt Justice calculates still repaid them more than Zambia's government lenders received. In 2023 Debt Justice estimated that private lenders holding the bonds of Ethiopia, Ghana, Sri Lanka, Suriname and Zambia could make $20 billion if paid in full on bonds bought when issued, or $30 billion on bonds bought at the low prices of that year.

The lenders' own portfolio has been counted once, by a campaigning organisation. In April 2016, days after the Panama Papers, Oxfam published an analysis of the companies that the International Finance Corporation, the World Bank's arm for lending to private business, had invested in in sub-Saharan Africa during 2015. Oxfam reported that 51 of those 68 companies used tax havens in ways with no apparent link to their core business, that the 51 received 84% of the IFC's investment in the region that year, and that IFC investment in companies using havens had risen from $1.20 billion in 2010 to $2.87 billion in 2015. That is Oxfam's reading of the IFC's own disclosures, not a figure the IFC publishes, and it has not been reproduced from the IFC's data here. At the Bank and IMF spring meetings that month the Bank's president, Jim Yong Kim, said the transfer of state assets to tax havens "can have a tremendous negative effect on our mission".

The largest award of all came from a mining dispute. On 12 July 2019 an ICSID tribunal ordered Pakistan to pay $5.976 billion to Tethyan Copper, owned by Canada's Barrick Gold and Chile's Antofagasta, after the province of Balochistan refused the company a mining lease at Reko Diq in November 2011 and Pakistan's Supreme Court declared the original agreement void in 2013. The award was $4.087 billion for the mine's value plus interest and costs, close to the size of the $6 billion loan the IMF had just agreed with Pakistan and equal to about 2 per cent of Pakistan's national income; Reuters reported the company had spent more than $220 million on the project, and its owners have put their spending above $500 million. In 2022 Pakistan settled: the award was dropped, Barrick took 50 per cent of a revived mine, and Pakistani state companies paid Antofagasta $900 million to leave.

How widespread the practice is cannot be counted, because no company has to publish what it pays to soldiers, police or armed groups abroad.

Chiquita paid a $25 million fine. The payments were demanded: they began after a meeting in 1997 at which the AUC's then leader, Carlos Castano, implied to a senior Banadex executive that failure to pay could result in physical harm to Banadex personnel and property, and when the company came forward it represented to the Justice Department that the payments had been made under threat of violence. Its own outside counsel advised that it could not do indirectly what it could not do directly, that a defence of duress would weaken if the payments continued, and that the company should leave Colombia; it stayed and kept paying.
